background.speaker: SPEAKER_01
background.text: Now, one of the things that you mentioned, North Star, one of the things that you pledged to do, and I mentioned this in my intro, is to, you know, ferret out corruption, end all dramatic privilege, change the ethical environment at City Hall. Have you succeeded in doing it? I'm sure you're going to say you have. Tell us how.

ground_truth: Look, I think we've taken some big steps forward. Two big things that we did very early on. As you may recall, my first day in office, I signed an executive order ending automatic prerogative across agencies in the city. And that was an important step, not only to send a message, but to really free up policymakers, people who were making the decisions about how resources were meted out across city departments, to free them up to do the right thing and not the political thing, and worry about whether or not the mayor was going to have their back when they were competing interests. And perhaps an alderman wanted to go in one direction, but they felt like what was in the best interest of the city was to go in a different direction. So that, I think, was a really big, important statement from day one. The other thing that we got done is there was ethics legislation that many members of the city council wanted to see passed. The former inspector general also wanted to see passed, but had been stalled under the previous administration. We got that done. And it's some of the most far-reaching of ethics reform that the city has really seen, not the least of which was giving the inspector general authority to investigate any issues related to alderman and city council committees. So those are some of the big things that we did. Now, look, I'm not going to sit here and tell you that we've rooted out all the vestiges of the machine. I'm also not going to tell you that one of the next big frontiers is in zoning, which is really also important for us to say, look, aldermen are important. Their voice is very important. But they cannot have unchecked veto power over how development happens or doesn't happen in the city of Chicago. So that's something that I think we're working our way towards. But I feel very good about it. And I think it's important for us to be able to tell the things that we've done. The other things that I think are important is we've tried to put more and more city data and be transparent out on the website from a dashboard that allows residents to see on a daily basis where things stand with public safety in their community, in a zip code, or across the city. That's really historic. And we did that a couple of years back. We have put a lot of other data out on the website. I'm out on websites and portals from various departments so that people don't have to FOIA to get information about how city government is functioning. So that's some of the list. But I feel very good. But look, I will share with you, Laura, I think one of the challenges that remains, and you did read the indictment of Ed Burke. But I suspect others didn't.

background.speaker: SPEAKER_01
background.text: okay now you mentioned earlier that um you've been you've been doing well in the polls and there's been a lot of polls in this race and some of them are not as reliable as others but one consistent thing that i've seen in the polls is that you you've had a pretty high disapproval rating among voters and that's that's a stark contrast to the first time you ran when you won every every war in the city and and part of that disapproval according to the polling and the commentary is that you can't you're not getting enough done because basically you're too hard to get along with that you're too mean how would you respond to that and and would you would you do anything different in your second term in terms of how you relate to people

background.speaker: [target]
background.text: Well, look, I always have to chuckle a little bit when I see that or hear that. And look, I know as a black woman, I'm always going to be viewed through a different lens. But the notion that I can't get anything done is ridiculous. You don't close an $838 million budget deficit, the largest in the history of our city, if you can't get things done and you can't collaborate. You don't get the casino done 30 years in the making, and we got that done on my watch. If you don't know how to collaborate, and frankly, I spent a lot of personal time working the phones, making the meetings with members of the General Assembly and leadership to get that done. Every single time that there's been a challenge that has faced our residents that required us to collaborate and get things done, we've made that. I'll expand it out to something even more recent. For decades, mayors have attempted to get an agreement with the surrounding Chicagoland counties to work together on marketing and business development. No mayors have ever been able to get that done. I got that done. Why were we able to get that done? Because of the personal relationships that I built with people who, frankly, most of whom I didn't know before I became the mayor of the city. But we spent a lot of time building trust. Building relationships. And that's made an enormous difference in our ability to work together as not just Chicago, acting upon the suburbs, but Chicagoland. I could give you a longer list, but the point is people may not like my delivery. I don't buy votes. I expect people and elected officials in particular to be the fiduciaries of the people they represent. And not just the residents in their ward. But the residents of their whole city. That rubs some people the wrong way. And look, I came into office not coming up through the machine, not being the person that somebody sent. But that's given me the independence that I think is necessary to be able to make the right calls, do the right thing for the right reasons, and not for politically expedient reasons. You asked the question of going into term two. I think we built a lot of really strong relationships. I think term two gives us the opportunity. To deepen those relationships and look for other opportunities to work together really across the board, not only with city council members, with stakeholders in the community, community organizations, the philanthropic community, and, of course, the business community.

background.speaker: SPEAKER_01
background.text: So deepen those relationships is going to be a goal of, you feel like you've forged them already. You're going to deepen them in the next term.

ground_truth: Yeah, I think that's right. I mean, look, there's no question whatsoever. Two years of really every day battling a global pandemic didn't give us a lot of time to be as, I think, broad and deep as I would have liked in building relationships and introducing myself to people that I may not have known before I took office. We built a lot of really deep relationships with the people who were on the front lines, our hospital systems, a number of different community-based that were advocating on behalf of vulnerable communities. Those relationships are deep and they are strong, and they are inuring to the benefit of our city to this day. Now we've, in the last year, when we're not out of the pandemic, I don't want to suggest that we are, but I've had much more freedom and opportunity to build those relationships, in person, build those relationships in other ways. And we're going to continue expanding that outreach to people and important stakeholders across the city.
